subskill: form: subject-verb agreement and auxiliary choice after a fronted negative adverb
passage: A pear orchard on dry upland soil serves as a test site for rootstocks bred to tolerate drought. Rarely during a dry summer in the orchard's upper terraces ______ youngest and least established grafted saplings grown more than a few centimeters, but this year a new rootstock carried them through August with almost no irrigation. Growers who toured the terraces in the fall were surprised by the length of the new shoots.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Because the sentence opens with "Rarely during a dry summer in the orchard's upper terraces," the auxiliary comes before its subject, "its youngest and least established grafted saplings." The head of that subject is "saplings," which is plural; the singular "summer" in the fronted phrase and the shared "its" (which refers to the orchard) do not set the number. The participle "grown" later in the sentence requires the perfect auxiliary "have"; "do" could combine only with the base form "grow." "has its" uses the right auxiliary but is singular, "do its" cannot combine with "grown," and "does its" fails on both counts.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement and possessive pronoun reference with split antecedents
passage: The hard outer coat of some seeds ______ tiny embryos from soil moisture until heat from a grass fire cracks the coat. Prairie restorers imitate the fire by rubbing such seeds against sandpaper before sowing, a step that can raise germination in the first spring from a few percent to nearly half.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of the verb is "coat"; "of some seeds" only modifies it, so the verb must be the singular "shields." The pronoun names the owner of "tiny embryos," and the embryos belong to the seeds, not to the coat, so the plural "their," referring to "some seeds," is needed. "shield their" makes the verb agree with the nearby "seeds" instead of "coat." "shields its" has the right verb but a pronoun that could only point to the coat, which has no embryos of its own, and "shield its" is wrong on both counts.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement and verb tense with a "many a" subject
passage: Measles can look quite different from the pictures in medical textbooks. Many a newly trained physician ______ slow to recognize the spots if the rash appears on darker skin, because the bright red blotches of textbook photographs show up there only as a faint, uneven roughness. For that reason, training materials should include photographs of patients with a wide range of skin tones.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "many a newly trained physician." Although "many" suggests a plural, "many a" is always followed by a singular noun and takes a singular verb. The tense is set inside the same sentence by the conditional clause "if the rash appears," whose present-tense verb requires a present-tense main verb. "are" treats "many" as plural, "was" is singular but past and clashes with "appears," and "were" is both plural and past.
topic_tag: medical education: measles rash on darker skin

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement and verb tense past an absolute phrase
passage: In neonatal units, infants born several weeks early are weaned from breathing support in small steps. The premature twins, a single sensor taped to the chest of the smaller infant, ______ without assistance or extra oxygen while the nurses review oxygen readings at the bedside. A dip in those readings means another day of support.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "the premature twins," which is plural. The phrase between the commas, "a single sensor taped to the chest of the smaller infant," is an absolute phrase with its own noun; neither "sensor" nor "infant" is the subject of the verb. The tense is set in the same sentence by "while the nurses review," a present-tense verb, so the main verb must also be present. "is breathing" agrees with "infant" instead of "twins," "were breathing" is plural but past and clashes with "review," and "was breathing" is wrong in both number and tense.
topic_tag: neonatology: weaning premature twins from oxygen

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement and verb tense with a comparative quantifier subject
passage: Chytrid fungus kills frogs by disrupting the way their skin absorbs water and salts. More swabs than a single laboratory can screen ______ to distant universities for analysis when the fungus appeared in the mountain lakes of one national park. Each swab must be tested for the fungus's DNA within a few days of collection.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "more swabs," which is plural; "than a single laboratory can screen" is the comparison, and "laboratory" is not the subject of the main verb. The tense is set later in the same sentence by "when the fungus appeared," a past-tense verb, so the main verb must be past; the present "can screen" belongs to the comparison and does not fix the main verb's tense. "was shipped" agrees with "laboratory," "are shipped" is plural but present and clashes with "appeared," and "is shipped" is wrong in both number and tense.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement and verb tense past an "or" gloss
passage: Soils that have lost most of their organic matter hold little water through a dry summer. Biochar, or the charred fragments of crop stalks heated in a sealed kiln, ______ across the most depleted fields of one district until the autumn rains return. A gram of biochar can hold several times its weight in water.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "biochar," which is singular. The words between the commas, "or the charred fragments of crop stalks heated in a sealed kiln," are a gloss that renames biochar; "or" here does not join two alternative subjects, so the plural "fragments" does not make the verb plural. The tense is set in the same sentence by "until the autumn rains return," whose present-tense verb requires a present main verb. "are being spread" agrees with "fragments," "was being spread" is singular but past and clashes with "return," and "were being spread" is wrong in both number and tense.
topic_tag: soil science: biochar on depleted fields

subskill: boundaries: comma before a coordinating "for" joining two independent clauses
passage: On upland sheep farms, the weeks when ewes give birth are the busiest stretch of the year. Shepherds keep pregnant ewes in a heated barn during the lambing ______ newborn lambs left in a cold field can lose dangerous amounts of body heat within an hour of birth. A barn also lets the shepherd check each ewe during the night.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "Shepherds keep pregnant ewes in a heated barn during the lambing season" is an independent clause, and "newborn lambs left in a cold field can lose dangerous amounts of body heat" is a second one; "for" here means "because" and joins them as a coordinating conjunction, which takes a comma before it. With no mark, "for newborn lambs" reads as a prepositional phrase attached to "season," and the sentence then runs into the verb "can lose" with no proper link. A semicolon or a colon placed before a coordinating conjunction is not the conventional way to join two clauses like these: "season; for" and "season: for" put a clause-ending mark in front of the word that already does the joining.

subskill: boundaries: no punctuation between the halves of a "both ... and" correlative
passage: Because ground beetles eat slugs and aphid eggs, many grain farmers leave margins of unplowed ground around their fields. One winter survey found the beetles sheltering both in the grassy strips that bordered the ______ the hedgerows along the farm lane, where a thick layer of leaf litter kept the soil from freezing.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The correlative "both ... and" pairs two prepositional phrases: "in the grassy strips that bordered the wheat" and "in the hedgerows along the farm lane." Even though the first phrase is long, because it contains the restrictive clause "that bordered the wheat," no punctuation separates the two halves of the pair. "wheat, and in" puts a comma between the paired elements; "wheat; and in" uses a semicolon, which must join independent clauses, but what follows is only a phrase; "wheat and, in" places a comma between "and" and the phrase it introduces.
topic_tag: pest management: ground beetles in field margins

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement after a fronted prepositional complement ("Of greater concern to the [plural]") with be-inversion and a plural postposed subject whose head is seven words after the verb, crossed with present versus past tense decided by a past-tense when-clause later in the same sentence
passage: When engineers plan to raise an aging concrete dam, cracks in its face are the obvious worry. Of greater concern to the drilling crews ______ thin, steeply tilted, and partly weathered seams of clay beneath the left abutment of one such dam when the first rock cores came up. Wet clay can lose much of its strength and let a heavier dam slide downstream.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The verb comes before its subject here: what was "Of greater concern" is "the thin, steeply tilted, and partly weathered seams of clay," whose head noun "seams" is plural, so the singular "concern" at the front of the sentence does not set the verb's number. The clause "when the first rock cores came up" places the whole sentence in the past, so the verb must be past: "were the." "are the" is plural but present, which clashes with "came up." "was the" is past but singular, agreeing with "concern" rather than "seams," and "is the" is both singular and present.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with "All that survives of the [plural]" as a singular subject, crossed with simple past passive versus present perfect passive decided by a definite-past when-clause in the same sentence
passage: Early seismographs are rare survivors, because their brass levers and smoked-glass plates break easily and their clockwork rusts in damp storerooms. All that survives of the first such instruments ______ into two padded crates when the hilltop observatory closed its doors. Curators can reconstruct how the machines worked from their gears, but the records they traced are lost.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "All that survives," in which "all" means "everything"; the singular verb "survives" inside it shows that it is singular, so the plural "instruments" beside the blank does not set the number. The clause "when the hilltop observatory closed its doors" names a definite moment in the past, and a verb tied to such a moment must be simple past rather than present perfect: "was packed." "has been packed" is singular but present perfect, which cannot be pinned to the moment named by "closed." "were packed" is past but plural, agreeing with "instruments," and "have been packed" is both plural and present perfect.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with "The former" resuming the singular first member of a mixed pair from the previous sentence, past a participial interrupter ending in a plural noun, crossed with present versus past passive decided by a present-tense whenever-clause in the same sentence
passage: A small weather station on an exposed mountain ridge can take all of its readings with just a single cup anemometer and two tipping-bucket rain gauges mounted close to the ground. The former, bolted to a steel mast high above the surrounding pines, ______ by technicians whenever a storm brings gusts strong enough to loosen bolts.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "The former" refers to the first of the two things named in the previous sentence, "a single cup anemometer," not to the "two tipping-bucket rain gauges," so it is singular; the plural "pines" at the end of the interrupting phrase "bolted to a steel mast high above the surrounding pines" is not the subject. The clause "whenever a storm brings gusts" describes a repeated present event, so the main verb must be present as well: "is checked." "are checked" is present but plural, agreeing with "pines" or with the gauges. "was checked" is singular but past, which clashes with "brings," and "were checked" is both plural and past.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a plural subject followed by a comma-set negated singular element ("Y, not X,") beside the verb, crossed with present versus past progressive decided by a past-tense as-clause in the same sentence
passage: A long, light footbridge can sway sideways even in calm air, because walkers unconsciously fall into step with its motion. The walkers' footsteps, not the steady breeze, ______ the handrails sideways as hundreds of people crossed a new river footbridge on opening day. Dampers fitted beneath a deck can absorb such motion.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "The walkers' footsteps," which is plural; "not the steady breeze" is set off by commas and only denies a second possible cause, so the singular "breeze" beside the blank does not control the verb. The clause "as hundreds of people crossed" places the action in the past, so the verb must be past progressive: "were shaking." "are shaking" is plural but present, which clashes with "crossed." "was shaking" is past but singular, agreeing with "breeze," and "is shaking" is both singular and present.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in a nonrestrictive partitive relative (", the longest of which") after a plural antecedent, crossed with present versus past progressive passive decided by a past-tense until-clause in the same sentence
passage: Moving freight through tunnels can clear heavy trucks from a crowded waterfront, but digging beneath a harbor is slow, costly, and risky work. Crews at one port bored four freight tunnels beneath the soft harbor floor, the longest of which ______ with precast concrete rings until groundwater broke through a weak joint.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of the relative clause is "the longest of which," meaning the longest single tunnel, so it is singular even though "which" stands for the plural "tunnels." The clause "until groundwater broke through a weak joint" places the lining work in the past, so the verb must be past: "was being lined." "is being lined" is singular but present, which clashes with "broke." "were being lined" is past but plural, agreeing with "tunnels," and "are being lined" is both plural and present.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement on the clause-final auxiliary of a non-inverted comparative than-clause with a plural subject, crossed with be versus do decided by the main clause's lexical verb
passage: Thick wind-blown loess holds rainwater far longer than the coarse, stony terraces on the lower slopes ______, so farmers on the plateau can often grow wheat without any irrigation. On the terraces, the same rain drains away within days. The difference explains why villages in the region cluster on the high ground rather than near the river.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The than-clause has its own subject, "the coarse, stony terraces on the lower slopes," whose head noun "terraces" is plural; the singular "loess" is the subject of the main clause, not of this one. The verb at the end of the than-clause stands in for the main clause's verb "holds," a lexical verb, so the substitute must be a form of "do," and the plural form is "do." "does" is the right kind of verb but singular, copying "loess holds." "are" is plural but a form of "be," which cannot stand in for "holds," and "is" is both singular and a form of "be."

subskill: boundaries: semicolon between two independent clauses where the second clause's subject is a bare quantifier pronoun ("most") right after a plural noun
passage: A brick lining for a steelmaking furnace must survive sudden cooling, an even harsher test than steady heat. To screen candidates, engineers dropped red-hot samples into cold water to compare six refractory ______ broke apart within seconds. Only a dense alumina blend came through whole, and the engineers chose it for the lining.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The words before the blank form an independent clause ending in "six refractory clays," and "most broke apart within seconds" is a second independent clause in which "most" is the subject of "broke." Two independent clauses with no conjunction need a semicolon between them: "clays; most." "clays, most" joins the clauses with only a comma, a comma splice; read as a phrase renaming "clays," it leaves "broke" without a subject. "clays most" runs the two clauses together with no mark at all. "clays, most," sets "most" off as an aside and again leaves "broke" with no subject.

subskill: boundaries: colon before a sentence-final list that names the members of the last item of a complete series
passage: To the eye, soil returned from the lunar highlands looks like plain gray powder. Its makeup matters, because the relative proportions of its minerals tell geologists which kind of ancient crust a sample came from. Under a microscope, each scoop reveals fine dust, glassy beads formed by meteorite impacts, and three common ______ pyroxene, and olivine.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The words before the blank are a complete clause whose object is itself a finished series, "fine dust, glassy beads formed by meteorite impacts, and three common minerals"; the words after the blank, "plagioclase, pyroxene, and olivine," name those three minerals. A colon after a complete clause can introduce such a list: "minerals: plagioclase." "minerals, plagioclase" merges the two lists into one series that contains "and" twice, so the minerals read as three more items rather than as the three just mentioned. "minerals; plagioclase" leaves a fragment after the semicolon, which must join two independent clauses. "minerals plagioclase" runs the list straight into the noun with no mark.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in a So + adverb + prepositional phrase inversion with a singular mass-noun subject placed after plural nouns in the fronted phrase, crossed with be versus do as the auxiliary decided by the -ing form after the subject
passage: Sociolinguists usually expect new words to travel slowly between neighborhoods, carried by family ties and shared workplaces. So quickly through secondary schools and their weekend sports leagues ______ and largely untraceable schoolyard slang spreading that researchers who record a term in one district often hear it in another within a month. The researchers attribute the pace to students who travel to play matches far from home.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of the inverted clause comes after the blank: it is "slang" ("new and largely untraceable schoolyard slang"), a singular noun, while "schools" and "leagues" sit inside the fronted phrase "So quickly through secondary schools and their weekend sports leagues" and cannot be the subject, so the auxiliary must be singular. The auxiliary must also be a form of "be": the verb that completes it, "spreading," is an -ing form, which combines with "is" ("is ... spreading"), whereas "does" would need the base form "spread." Only "is new" is both singular and a form of "be." "are new" has the right auxiliary but is plural, agreeing with "leagues." "does new" is singular but cannot combine with "spreading," and "do new" is both plural and the wrong auxiliary.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in a nonrestrictive which-clause whose antecedent is a both ... and compound of two singular nouns, crossed with present versus past progressive passive decided by a present-tense verb in a while-clause of the same sentence
passage: A regional museum acquired both the painted altarpiece and the carved choir screen, which ______ in the museum's basement workshop side by side while conservators who suspect a single painter compare their pigments layer by layer. A close match would suggest that one workshop produced both pieces for the same chapel, a conclusion that would overturn the attribution printed in the guides to the church.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The relative pronoun "which" refers to the whole compound "both the painted altarpiece and the carved choir screen," two works, so the verb must be plural; "screen," the singular noun just before the comma, is only the second of the two, and the works are restored "side by side," which one object alone cannot be. The verb must also be present, because the restoration happens at the same time as the present-tense "compare" in the while-clause ("while conservators ... compare their pigments"). Only "are being restored" is plural and present. "is being restored" is present but singular, as if "which" referred to "screen" alone. "were being restored" is plural but past, which clashes with "compare" even though the museum "acquired" the works in the past, and "was being restored" is both singular and past.
topic_tag: technical art history: matching pigments across church furnishings

subskill: form: subject-verb and pronoun-antecedent agreement with a singular head noun followed by a content clause whose own plural subject and plural verb come before the blank, verb and possessive pronoun both referring to the head
passage: Two sections of a medieval choirbook differ sharply in their handwriting but share an unusual system of musical notation. The hypothesis that the book's two scribes were trained in a single convent workshop ______ plausibility mainly to that notation, which appears in no other surviving manuscript from the region. Without it, scholars would have little reason to connect the two hands at all.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of the main clause is "hypothesis"; "that the book's two scribes were trained in a single convent workshop" is a clause stating what the hypothesis claims, and its own subject "scribes" (with its plural verb "were trained") is not the subject of the blank, so the verb must be the singular "owes." The pronoun must also refer to "hypothesis," because only a hypothesis can have plausibility owed to evidence; the scribes do not, so the pronoun is the singular "its." Only "owes its" is right on both counts. "owes their" has the right verb but a plural pronoun that would point to "scribes." "owe its" has the right pronoun but a plural verb agreeing with "scribes," and "owe their" makes both errors.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a compound subject that names one person under a single determiner, crossed with past versus present progressive decided by a past-tense when-clause in the same sentence
passage: Many farm names in the county survive only in the memories of elderly residents, never having been written on any map. The founder and first director of the county place-name survey ______ a list of the abandoned farm names in the hills when she suffered the illness that ended her fieldwork, and no one completed the list after her. Her notebooks are kept at the county library.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "The founder and first director of the county place-name survey" names a single person, as the single determiner "The" and the later "she" and "her fieldwork" show, so the subject is singular despite "and" and the verb must be singular. The verb must also be past, because the compiling was under way at the moment named by the past-tense when-clause "when she suffered the illness that ended her fieldwork." Only "was compiling" is singular and past. "were compiling" is past but plural, treating the founder and the director as two people. "is compiling" is singular but present, which cannot describe an activity in progress when a past illness ended it, and "are compiling" is both plural and present.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement on the clause-final verb of a concessive Adjective + as + subject clause, with the main clause's singular subject right after the blank, crossed with present versus past decided by the main clause's present-tense verb
passage: A hill-town church holds two fresco cycles painted by a single workshop. Faded as the frescoes in the two side chapels ______, the subject of each scene is easy to identify for any visitor who knows the stories they illustrate. The painters outlined each figure in a dark earth pigment that resists light far better than the colors laid over it.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The blank is the verb of the concessive clause "Faded as the frescoes in the two side chapels ______," whose subject is "frescoes," a plural noun; "subject," the singular noun that follows the comma, belongs to the main clause, so the verb must be plural. The verb must also be present: the concession describes the frescoes' condition at the same time as the main clause's present-tense "is easy to identify," and the fading is set against that present ease. Only "are" is plural and present. "is" is present but singular, as if "subject" were its subject. "were" is plural but places the fading in a past that the present-tense main clause does not share, and "was" is both singular and past.
topic_tag: fresco painting: outlined figures in a hill-town church

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement after a fronted (topicalized) singular object, with the plural subject just before the blank, crossed with past progressive versus present perfect progressive decided by a definite-past when-clause in the same sentence
passage: Most of the merchant house's account books were photographed and returned to storage without being read. This last ledger the two archivists ______ line by line, checking each debt against the surviving letters, when a burst pipe flooded the reading room and soaked the binding. Conservators later dried the pages, but several columns of figures are lost.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "This last ledger" is the object of the verb, moved to the front of the sentence; the subject is "the two archivists," a plural, so the verb must be plural even though the sentence opens with a singular noun. The verb must also be the past progressive, not the present perfect progressive, because the transcribing was interrupted at a definite past moment, "when a burst pipe flooded the reading room," and the present perfect cannot be tied to a definite past time. Only "were transcribing" is plural and past progressive. "have been transcribing" is plural but present perfect, which clashes with "when a burst pipe flooded." "was transcribing" is past but singular, agreeing with "ledger," and "has been transcribing" is both singular and present perfect.
topic_tag: business history: a merchant house's ledgers

subskill: boundaries: a dash pair, both marks supplied, around an appositive list that itself contains commas, between a subject noun and its verb
passage: Touring opera troupes rarely kept their stage properties after a season ended, so few such objects reach museums intact. One troupe's surviving ______ kept in a single cedar trunk, which a descendant of its last manager gave to a regional theater museum. Curators display the trunk open so that visitors can see how tightly the pieces were packed for travel.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: props, a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon, are
props—a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon—are
props a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon are
props—a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon, are
correct_answer: props—a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon—are
explanation: The subject is "One troupe's surviving props," its verb is "are kept," and between them sits an appositive list naming the props, "a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon," which already contains commas. Because the list has internal commas, it must be set off by two matching dashes, as in "props—a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon—are." The comma pair in "props, a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon, are" makes the props read as a fourth item in one long list and then puts a comma between that subject and its verb. "props—a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon, are" opens with a dash but closes with a comma, so the interruption is never properly closed. "props a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon are" runs the noun "props" straight into the list with nothing to show that the list renames it.
topic_tag: theater history: a touring opera troupe's props

subskill: boundaries: a restrictive appositive (role + name) with no commas, in a passage that establishes several holders of the role
passage: Three engravers cut the copper plates for the first printed atlas of the coast, and the publisher paid each of them by the plate. Of the three, only the ______ signed his plates, so the work of the other two can be told apart solely by the style of their lettering. Historians have matched that lettering to two later almanacs.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The name "Vidal" identifies which of the three engravers is meant, so it is a restrictive appositive and takes no commas: "only the engraver Vidal signed his plates." The comma pair in "engraver, Vidal," would make the name extra information about a single, already identified engraver, but the passage has just said there were three, so "the engraver" alone does not pick one out. "engraver Vidal," puts a comma between the subject "the engraver Vidal" and its verb "signed." "engraver, Vidal" opens a nonrestrictive interruption with a comma and never closes it.
topic_tag: history of engraving: a coastal atlas
